screens.title: What triggers a replica set election?
screens.narratorSegment: An election starts when the existing primary is no longer considered reachable by a majority of the other members or when an administrator intentionally steps down the primary. Reachability means the other members can communicate with the primary and confirm its state; if network partitions, host failure, or process crashes prevent that, the cluster may detect the primary as unavailable. Manual stepdown is an administrative action that forces the primary to relinquish leadership, immediately prompting an election. The majority requirement is important: a candidate cannot become primary unless more than half of the voting members endorse it. For example, in a three-member replica set, at least two votes are required. That rule prevents split-brain—two nodes mistakenly thinking they are both primary—and keeps writes consistent. A common misconception is that any single surviving secondary can always become primary; in fact, without a majority of voting members available, no election can succeed and writes will remain unavailable. In practice you should plan for node failures and network partitions by keeping an odd number of voting members and ensuring monitoring alerts are in place. Reflect on how often your environment could lose network connectivity between datacenters and whether your voting topology supports safe elections.

keyIdea.title: Trigger summary
keyIdea.text: Elections are triggered by primary unreachability or manual stepdown and require a majority of voting members to succeed.

content.html:
Core Concept
What triggers an election?
An election starts when the primary becomes unreachable to a majority or when an admin steps it down.
Primary unreachable
Network partition, process crash, or host outage can make the primary appear dead.
Manual stepdown
An administrator forces a primary to step down, immediately prompting an election.
No majority
If a candidate cannot get a majority of votes, the replica set will remain without a primary.
Key Takeaway

Majority reachability is the gatekeeper for elections. Without it, no member can become primary and writes are unavailable.

Example scenario
In a three-member set, if the primary fails and the secondaries can both see each other, one will become primary after a vote. If a network split leaves just one secondary isolated, it cannot elect itself because it lacks majority.
  • Definition: Election — process to choose a primary when needed.
  • Misconception: A single remaining secondary can always win — false without majority.
  • Why it matters: Prevents split-brain and preserves data consistency.
Check your understanding
If your two data centers each host two voting members and one center loses networking, can the other center elect a primary? Think about majority across total voting members.

screens.title: Nomination and voting process
screens.narratorSegment: When a primary is gone, the secondaries move into an election state where eligible members may nominate themselves as candidates. A candidate broadcasts its candidacy and requests votes from voting members. Each member evaluating a request considers whether the candidate is reachable, has up-to-date data, and is eligible based on configuration such as votes and priority. Voting members respond and the candidate tallies votes; to win it must secure a majority of votes from all voting members. The chapter describes this as a variant of consensus algorithms—MongoDB's internal variant—whose practical effect is the same: the system avoids simultaneous primaries. A clear example: in a five-member deployment with four remaining nodes after one failure, a candidate needs at least three votes to win. A subtle point is the difference between all members and voting members: only voting members are counted when determining majority. Misconfiguring hidden members or votes can cause fewer voting members than expected, impairing elections. Finally, understand that reachability to a majority is also checked: a candidate must be able to communicate with a majority to accept step-in. Consider how timeouts and network delay might delay elections and how that would surface in monitoring.

keyIdea.title: Election steps
keyIdea.text: A candidate announces itself, requests votes, voting members respond, and a majority of votes from voting members is required to win.

content.html:
Process Flow
Nomination and voting
1
Nomination
An eligible secondary declares candidacy and broadcasts that intention to other members.
2
Vote requests
The candidate sends vote requests; recipients assess reachability and data currency before casting a vote.
3
Majority decision
If the candidate gets a majority of voting members' votes, it becomes primary and starts accepting writes.
Supporting notes
  • Only members with votes:1 participate in the vote tally.
  • Oplog currency is checked to prefer the most up-to-date candidate.
  • The candidate must be reachable and be able to contact a majority.
Analogy
Think of members as a jury: a candidate needs the majority of jurors who are allowed to vote to reach a verdict.
Key Takeaway

Elections are a coordinated request-and-vote process that requires both eligibility and majority agreement among voting members.

screens.title: Majority, voting members, and split-brain
screens.narratorSegment: Majority is the central safety property of replica set elections. A candidate must receive more than half of the votes from eligible voting members to become primary. That majority rule prevents split-brain, in which two members mistakenly assume leadership simultaneously, because two different candidates cannot each secure a majority when a majority is a single consistent set of voting members. It's important to distinguish between total members and voting members: some members can be configured with votes:0 and will not count toward the majority. A frequent mistake is to reduce the count of voting members inadvertently — for example, by marking extra hidden or arbiter nodes incorrectly — which changes the majority threshold and can cause unexpected election outcomes. Consider the example of a two-voter deployment: if one fails, the remaining single voter cannot form a majority by itself and no new primary can be elected. That produces full write unavailability until more voters are reachable. In practice, aim for at least three voting members and make vote configuration intentional. Ask yourself whether any node you made non-voting should actually be able to help the cluster elect a new primary during failures.

keyIdea.title: Safety rule
keyIdea.text: A majority of voting members is required to elect a primary; misconfiguring votes can reduce availability and risk split-brain avoidance failures.

content.html:
Comparison
Voting members vs non-voting members
Voting member (votes:1)
Participates in elections; counts toward majority.
Non-voting member (votes:0)
Does not vote; useful for hidden or reporting nodes that shouldn’t affect elections.
Scenarios
  • 3 voting members: one failure still allows a majority (2 of 3).
  • 2 voting members: failure of one prevents a majority and blocks elections.
  • Hidden non-voting nodes do not help elect a primary despite contributing replication capacity.
Misconception
Adding more total nodes always increases availability — false if those nodes are non-voting, they do not improve election quorum.
Key Takeaway

Design voting topology intentionally: prefer odd numbers of voting members and ensure votes are set to reflect each node's role in availability.

screens.title: Priority and how it influences elections
screens.narratorSegment: Priority is a configuration setting that influences which replica set members are preferred as primary. Each member has a priority value (default 1); higher priority members are more likely to become primary when an election occurs. You can set priority to zero for members that should never become primary, such as dedicated reporting nodes or offsite disaster recovery replicas. Priority does not guarantee election victory if the member's oplog is not up-to-date or it cannot reach a majority. In other words, priority biases the election but does not override data currency or reachability requirements. A common misstep is to assign very high priority to a node that is network-isolated or slow to catch up, which can cause longer failovers or increased replication lag when it wins leadership. Practical use: set priority to zero for nodes that must never accept writes, and distribute higher priorities to nodes in locations where you want leadership. Remember, priority is just one of several factors—votes and oplog currency remain decisive when comparing candidates. Priority and how it influences elections means higher priority increases the chance of being elected, but does not override oplog currency or reachability requirements; priority:0 prevents a member from becoming primary.. In practical terms, controlling which members are preferred for primary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept
Priority and election bias
Priority values indicate which members are preferred for primary selection but they are not absolute guarantees.
priority: >0
Member is eligible and its higher value increases selection probability.
priority: 0
Member will not be elected primary; useful for reporting or disaster recovery nodes.
Concrete example
If you have a fast, local data center node you prefer as primary, give it a higher priority. But ensure it also keeps its oplog current; otherwise a slower but more up-to-date node may be preferred at election time.
Misconception
Higher priority will always win — incorrect. Oplog currency and reachability are required in addition to priority.
Key Takeaway

Use priority to steer leadership, but balance it with replication health. priority:0 protects nodes from accidental leadership.

screens.title: Oplog currency and data safety
screens.narratorSegment: Oplog currency describes how current a member's operation log is relative to the former primary. During elections the replica set prefers candidates with the most up-to-date oplog to minimize potential data loss. That means a secondary that has applied the latest writes will be a stronger candidate than a lagging node, even if the lagging node has equal priority. This preference helps preserve durability guarantees across failover: the new primary should reflect as much of the old primary's acknowledged writes as possible. A common confusion is thinking priority alone ensures the freshest data; in reality, a candidate must also have up-to-date oplog entries and be reachable to a majority. Practically, monitor replication lag and oplog window to ensure secondaries can catch up quickly. If your fastest priority node lags frequently, consider reducing its priority or improving replication performance so it won't prolong elections or increase the chance of data loss. Always balance leader preference with actual replication health to safeguard consistency. Oplog currency and data safety means oplog currency prevents data loss by preferring the candidate closest to the former primary's state when electing a new primary.. In practical terms, why the most up-to-date candidate is preferred. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Oplog rule
keyIdea.text: Oplog currency prevents data loss by preferring the candidate closest to the former primary's state when electing a new primary.

content.html:
Definition
Oplog currency
A measure of how current a member's oplog is compared to the previous primary. Higher currency reduces potential data loss after failover.
Why it matters
Choosing the most current candidate minimizes missing acknowledged writes after promotion.
Operational tip
Monitor replication lag and oplog windows so secondaries can keep up during failovers.
Concrete example
If Node A has applied the last 100 writes and Node B is behind by 50 writes, Node A is preferred for election even if both have equal priority.
Misconception
Priority alone ensures freshness — false. Oplog currency is required as well.
Key Takeaway

Promote nodes that are up-to-date. Ensure replication keeps pace so preferred primaries truly reflect the latest state.

screens.title: Votes and voting member configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Votes determine which members participate in elections and therefore shape the quorum required to elect a primary. Members configured with votes:1 can cast ballots; members with votes:0 do not participate. Hidden or reporting nodes are commonly set to votes:0 to exclude them from quorum calculations while still receiving replicated data. When planning quorum, remember that the majority is defined over voting members. For example, if your replica set has five members but two are configured as votes:0, your majority is calculated over the three voting members only. A common configuration error is unintentionally setting votes:0 on too many nodes, reducing the number of voters and making majority harder to attain after failures. Conversely, sprinkling votes across many geographic regions without considering network partitions can make it possible that no single region has a majority if links fail. The practical guidance is to keep voting members stable, use votes:0 for non-leadership nodes intentionally, and document the quorum topology so recovery behavior is predictable during incidents. Votes and voting member configuration means only voting members count toward majority; misconfiguring votes changes quorum and can cause unexpected unavailability.. In practical terms, who can vote and how votes affect quorum. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Voting members and quorum
Voting members (votes:1) cast ballots during elections. Quorum and majority are computed over voting members only.
votes:1
Participates in election; contributes to majority.
votes:0
Does not vote; useful for hidden or reporting members.
Example
Five members with two non-voting results in three voting members; majority is two. After a failure you need the remaining voters to form a majority.
Operational tip
Document which nodes are voting and why, and avoid changing votes in the heat of an incident without plan.
Common Mistake

Having only two voting members can prevent elections after one fails. Use at least three voting members for safe availability.

screens.title: Reachability and availability during elections
screens.narratorSegment: Reachability is both a precondition for voting and an ongoing requirement for a candidate to assume leadership. A candidate must be able to communicate with a majority of members during the election sequence; if network partitions isolate a candidate from enough members, it cannot win even if it has higher priority and a current oplog. Availability can be impacted by transient network issues: small delays can lengthen elections while extended partitions may prevent any primary from being elected. This leads to a practical approach: test your network topology under failure scenarios, and avoid placing a majority of voting members across unreliable network links. A common misconception is that increasing timeouts will always help elections succeed; while raising timeouts makes the system more tolerant to latency, it also prolongs the time the cluster is without a primary. Balance your timeouts and topology to reduce the window of unavailability while ensuring correct election outcomes. Finally, monitor reachability and alert on inter-node communication failures so you can react before they lead to unplanned downtime. Reachability and availability during elections means candidates must be able to reach a majority during elections; network topology and timeouts directly affect election success and failover duration.. In practical terms, why being able to communicate matters as much as config values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Reachability & availability
Network reachability determines whether candidates can contact voters and whether an election can succeed.

screens.title: Automatic failover lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Automatic failover includes a series of observable states: detection of primary unavailability, election among secondaries, election success, and reconfiguration after promotion. First, members detect that the primary is unreachable and mark it DOWN or UNKNOWN depending on observation intervals. Second, eligible secondaries begin candidacy and request votes. Third, when a candidate receives a majority of votes from voting members, it assumes the primary role and begins accepting write operations. Fourth, the former primary, when it recovers, rejoins as a secondary. For applications, the key impact is a brief window during which no primary is available and writes are rejected. The duration varies with network conditions, election timeout settings, and replication lag. Drivers that are properly configured with multiple seed hosts and the replicaSet name typically detect the new primary and reconnect, resuming operations. During this process, strict write concerns such as w:majority may block until a new majority forms. Understanding the sequence helps you instrument monitoring and implement retry logic that gives drivers time to discover the new primary and complete operations successfully. Automatic failover lifecycle means detection → election → promotion → rejoin; applications must handle the short window when no primary exists and be prepared to retry writes.. In practical terms, from primary failure to new primary acceptance of writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: How drivers handle primary changes
screens.narratorSegment: Modern MongoDB drivers automatically detect topology changes and attempt to route operations to the currently elected primary, but they require correct connection configuration to do so. The recommended pattern is to include multiple seed hosts and the replicaSet name in the connection string. That way, if the primary changes, the driver has alternate hosts to discover the current primary. During an election, the driver may surface transient errors; your application should differentiate between transient 'no primary available' errors and permanent failures, and implement retries with a short backoff. Be mindful of server selection timeouts: making them too short can cause frequent connection errors in unstable networks, while making them too long increases the perceived downtime when the topology actually changes. Also remember that strict write concerns like w:majority can block until a new majority forms, so coordinate retry policies with your application's tolerance for write latency and durability. Definition
Driver behavior and connection pattern
Include multiple seed hosts and the replicaSet option so the driver can discover the current primary after topology changes.
Example connection string
mongodb://host1:27017,host2:27018,host3:27019/?replicaSet=rs0
  • Driver discovers topology from the seeds and monitors for primary changes.

If the primary at host1 fails and the driver connected to host1 only, the driver cannot discover the new primary. With multiple seeds the driver contacts the remaining hosts and finds the current primary.

Configure drivers with multiple seeds and replicaSet name. Combine that with retries to tolerate short election windows.

screens.title: Strategies to minimize downtime during failovers
screens.narratorSegment: Minimizing downtime during failover requires both cluster configuration and application-level practices. On the cluster side, ensure you have at least three voting members and place them so that a single network partition cannot deny majority to all remaining nodes. Set priority values sensibly: prefer local, well-resourced nodes for leadership but only if they maintain up-to-date oplogs. Keep votes and priorities documented so operators understand the quorum. On the application side, use connection strings with multiple seed hosts and replicaSet name, implement retry logic for transient 'no primary available' errors, and consider the trade-offs of server selection timeouts. Also keep drivers updated because newer versions frequently improve failover detection and recovery. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how a MongoDB replica set detects a failed primary and elects a replacement automatically. Elections are the mechanism that preserves high availability: when a primary becomes unavailable or an administrator steps it down, the remaining members move through a short consensus process to choose a new primary. You will understand the conditions that trigger an election, the nomination and voting steps, and the practical factors—priority, votes, and oplog currency—that influence the winner. We'll also cover how modern drivers handle primary changes so your application can resume writes, plus strategies you can use to minimize downtime during those brief transition windows. A concrete example you will see repeatedly is a three-member replica set where a single primary failure causes the two remaining members to vote and form a new primary; that simple scenario highlights majority rules and common pitfalls like incorrect vote counts or improper priority values. By the end you'll be able to explain why at least three voting members are recommended, how write concerns interact with failover, and what to tune to reduce application disruption. Consider how your own deployment would behave if the primary stopped responding right now.

By the end of this chapter you will explain when a replica set election happens, describe the nomination and voting steps, identify factors that influence who becomes primary, and understand how automatic failover affects application connectivity. First, you will be able to name the conditions that trigger an election such as a primary becoming unreachable or a manual stepdown, and you will explain why a majority vote is required. Second, you will describe how candidates broadcast candidacy and request votes, and how voting is restricted to eligible voting members. Third, you will analyze how member settings like priority and oplog currency bias election outcomes and why you might set priority to zero for reporting nodes. Finally, you will explain how drivers handle primary changes and list strategies your application can use to minimize downtime during failovers. Each objective includes a concise practice cue: check rs. status during a simulated failure, and verify your driver reconnects when the new primary is elected.

This follow-up objectives slide expands how you'll practice each skill. You'll run rs. status checks to observe when the primary changes state, read election results to confirm which members voted, and interpret oplog timestamps to judge oplog currency. You'll also learn to confirm vote configurations (votes: 0 or 1) so you know which members can participate in elections. On the application side, you'll test driver behavior by connecting with multiple seed hosts and a replicaSet name, then observe how the driver reroutes operations after an election. Finally, you'll practice setting member priority to control leadership candidates and simulate how an offsite reporting node with priority zero never becomes primary. Together these objective drills give you hands-on checks and practical cues to both diagnose and reduce failover impact in production-like environments.

An election starts when the existing primary is no longer considered reachable by a majority of the other members or when an administrator intentionally steps down the primary. Reachability means the other members can communicate with the primary and confirm its state; if network partitions, host failure, or process crashes prevent that, the cluster may detect the primary as unavailable. Manual stepdown is an administrative action that forces the primary to relinquish leadership, immediately prompting an election. The majority requirement is important: a candidate cannot become primary unless more than half of the voting members endorse it. For example, in a three-member replica set, at least two votes are required. That rule prevents split-brain—two nodes mistakenly thinking they are both primary—and keeps writes consistent. A common misconception is that any single surviving secondary can always become primary; in fact, without a majority of voting members available, no election can succeed and writes will remain unavailable. In practice you should plan for node failures and network partitions by keeping an odd number of voting members and ensuring monitoring alerts are in place. Reflect on how often your environment could lose network connectivity between datacenters and whether your voting topology supports safe elections.

When a primary is gone, the secondaries move into an election state where eligible members may nominate themselves as candidates. A candidate broadcasts its candidacy and requests votes from voting members. Each member evaluating a request considers whether the candidate is reachable, has up-to-date data, and is eligible based on configuration such as votes and priority. Voting members respond and the candidate tallies votes; to win it must secure a majority of votes from all voting members. The chapter describes this as a variant of consensus algorithms—MongoDB's internal variant—whose practical effect is the same: the system avoids simultaneous primaries. A clear example: in a five-member deployment with four remaining nodes after one failure, a candidate needs at least three votes to win. A subtle point is the difference between all members and voting members: only voting members are counted when determining majority. Misconfiguring hidden members or votes can cause fewer voting members than expected, impairing elections. Finally, understand that reachability to a majority is also checked: a candidate must be able to communicate with a majority to accept step-in. Consider how timeouts and network delay might delay elections and how that would surface in monitoring.

Majority is the central safety property of replica set elections. A candidate must receive more than half of the votes from eligible voting members to become primary. That majority rule prevents split-brain, in which two members mistakenly assume leadership simultaneously, because two different candidates cannot each secure a majority when a majority is a single consistent set of voting members. It's important to distinguish between total members and voting members: some members can be configured with votes:0 and will not count toward the majority. A frequent mistake is to reduce the count of voting members inadvertently — for example, by marking extra hidden or arbiter nodes incorrectly — which changes the majority threshold and can cause unexpected election outcomes. Consider the example of a two-voter deployment: if one fails, the remaining single voter cannot form a majority by itself and no new primary can be elected. That produces full write unavailability until more voters are reachable. In practice, aim for at least three voting members and make vote configuration intentional. Ask yourself whether any node you made non-voting should actually be able to help the cluster elect a new primary during failures.

Priority is a configuration setting that influences which replica set members are preferred as primary. Each member has a priority value (default 1); higher priority members are more likely to become primary when an election occurs. You can set priority to zero for members that should never become primary, such as dedicated reporting nodes or offsite disaster recovery replicas. Priority does not guarantee election victory if the member's oplog is not up-to-date or it cannot reach a majority. In other words, priority biases the election but does not override data currency or reachability requirements. A common misstep is to assign very high priority to a node that is network-isolated or slow to catch up, which can cause longer failovers or increased replication lag when it wins leadership. Practical use: set priority to zero for nodes that must never accept writes, and distribute higher priorities to nodes in locations where you want leadership. Remember, priority is just one of several factors—votes and oplog currency remain decisive when comparing candidates. Priority and how it influences elections means higher priority increases the chance of being elected, but does not override oplog currency or reachability requirements; priority:0 prevents a member from becoming primary.. In practical terms, controlling which members are preferred for primary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Oplog currency describes how current a member's operation log is relative to the former primary. During elections the replica set prefers candidates with the most up-to-date oplog to minimize potential data loss. That means a secondary that has applied the latest writes will be a stronger candidate than a lagging node, even if the lagging node has equal priority. This preference helps preserve durability guarantees across failover: the new primary should reflect as much of the old primary's acknowledged writes as possible. A common confusion is thinking priority alone ensures the freshest data; in reality, a candidate must also have up-to-date oplog entries and be reachable to a majority. Practically, monitor replication lag and oplog window to ensure secondaries can catch up quickly. If your fastest priority node lags frequently, consider reducing its priority or improving replication performance so it won't prolong elections or increase the chance of data loss. Always balance leader preference with actual replication health to safeguard consistency. Votes determine which members participate in elections and therefore shape the quorum required to elect a primary. Members configured with votes:1 can cast ballots; members with votes:0 do not participate. Hidden or reporting nodes are commonly set to votes:0 to exclude them from quorum calculations while still receiving replicated data. When planning quorum, remember that the majority is defined over voting members. For example, if your replica set has five members but two are configured as votes:0, your majority is calculated over the three voting members only. A common configuration error is unintentionally setting votes:0 on too many nodes, reducing the number of voters and making majority harder to attain after failures. Conversely, sprinkling votes across many geographic regions without considering network partitions can make it possible that no single region has a majority if links fail. The practical guidance is to keep voting members stable, use votes:0 for non-leadership nodes intentionally, and document the quorum topology so recovery behavior is predictable during incidents. Minimizing downtime during failover requires both cluster configuration and application-level practices. On the cluster side, ensure you have at least three voting members and place them so that a single network partition cannot deny majority to all remaining nodes. Here are the essential concepts to remember from this chapter. First, an election is the process by which replica set members choose a new primary when the current primary becomes unavailable. Second, automatic failover is the end-to-end transition from one primary to another without manual intervention, though applications will see a short period with no primary. Third, majority is the quorum rule: a candidate must receive more than half of the votes from eligible voting members to win. Keep these concepts in mind when you design topology and operational playbooks because they govern when your cluster can accept writes and how quickly it recovers from failure. Three more short definitions to keep clear. Priority is a member setting that biases election selection; higher numbers make a node more likely to become primary, while priority:0 ensures a node never leads. Oplog currency measures how current a node's operation log is relative to the former primary; elections prefer the most current candidate to reduce data loss. Split-brain is a dangerous scenario where two members think they are primary, potentially causing divergent writes; majority rules prevent split-brain when voting is configured correctly. Make these distinctions when tuning your cluster: priority steers leadership, oplog currency protects data, and majority prevents split-brain.
